output.title: Design dashboards so neglect shows up fast
output.body:
Dashboard neglect is usually not a software problem first. It is a control problem: there is a screen, report, or approval view that should guide a recurring decision, but nobody checks it often enough to keep the work moving. For a small business, the useful question is not whether AI can read the dashboard. It is what happens when the owner does not look at it for two days.

A bounded way to design against that is to separate three responses. First, add a reminder if the owner simply forgets. Second, automate the data refresh so the dashboard stays current without manual copy-paste. Third, only consider a workflow handoff if the rule is clear and human approval stays in place for money movement and other high-risk calls. That gate stays human. The machine can carry the clipboard; it should not sign the cheque.

One practical next step is to pick one recurring dashboard the business already relies on and write a plain-English rule for it: what input arrives, what status changes, and what action follows. If the rule is fuzzy, stop at data collection. If it is clear, the pilot scope stays narrow. A simple example would be invoices that need follow-up, but that is only an example, not a claim about your business. Bareni’s policy is to hand work back into the owner’s own accounts and tools, with no-lock-in as positioning, not a warranty.
